That approach feels more like a patch than a real privacy model.

True confidentiality starts deeper, with infrastructure designed so privacy is part of the default experience rather than something added afterward.

That’s the direction Beldex is taking.

Instead of relying on separate companies for private messaging, secure browsing, and VPN services, the @BeldexCoin ecosystem brings these products together through a shared decentralized foundation.

The masternodes that support Beldex’s network also help power its product infrastructure.

They aren’t simply there to validate blocks. They play an active role across the ecosystem.

With BChat, users get a 64 character ID without needing an email address or SMS verification.

BelNet takes a decentralized routing approach, sending connections through randomized paths rather than relying on a traditional centralized VPN provider.

And at the blockchain layer, transactions use privacy-focused cryptography designed to conceal sensitive transaction details.

The bigger idea is simple:

Privacy works best when it’s built into the architecture from the start, not added as a feature after everything else is already in place.

Your whereabouts and data remain entirely private, by design.

title:
Microsoft is embedding a hidden tracking identifier in every AI-generated image you create using Paint or Photos on Windows.

A researcher discovered that these apps embed a server-issued GUID (a glob
content:
Microsoft is embedding a hidden tracking identifier in every AI-generated image you create using Paint or Photos on Windows.

A researcher discovered that these apps embed a server-issued GUID (a globally unique identifier) as an invisible watermark in locally generated AI images.

The watermark is tied to the prompts you type. And since those prompts are associated with your Microsoft account, Microsoft could "theoretically" trace any watermarked image back to the user who created it.

This is recycling an idea from the 80s. Back then, laser printer manufacturers added tiny yellow dot patterns to every printed page. With this, they could identify the printer.

Now Microsoft has brought the same idea to AI image generation, and added it to two of the most widely used default Windows apps.

Microsoft had disclosed its AI safety measures in official documentation, but the practical implication, that your output image file carries an invisible fingerprint linked to your identity, was never clearly mentioned, of course.

The researcher found this by reading Microsoft's own published documentation and analyzing the watermarking mechanics.

AI watermarking is a requirement by law in the EU. But "this image was generated by AI" is different than "this image was generated by AI by Mr. Winston Smith".

For anyone who values privacy, this is something to worry about. If you generate an image locally, on your own device, why should it carry a tag that can identify you to the company whose software you used?

But then, anyone who values their privacy won't be using Microsoft Windows anyway.

title: Grok Build just got a huge upgrade to the entire agentic coding experience......more powerful workflows with agent budget + reasoning controls, plugin-provided agents, image feedback, instant TUI mode
content:
Grok Build just got a huge upgrade to the entire agentic coding experience......more powerful workflows with agent budget + reasoning controls, plugin-provided agents, image feedback, instant TUI mode switching, smarter cloning and worktrees, more resilient subagents, faster MCP startup, and concurrent agents that can run hard without collapsing into rate-limit errors

Release Notes: v1.0.9

Features:
• New sessions in the interactive TUI now start in auto mode by default for fewer approval prompts.
• /feedback now supports attaching images (screenshots etc.).
• The / slash menu is now ordered by recency and groups skills below commands for easier navigation.
• /workflow now accepts --agent-budget N or an agent_budget JSON field to set child-agent limits.
• /workflow now accepts --effort LEVEL or an effort JSON field to set child reasoning effort.
• MCP servers now receive a grok-cli User-Agent header so providers can attribute traffic.
• Dashboard now lets you start new agents in Auto mode via Shift+Tab.
• Workflows now appear alongside skills in the model prompt so the agent can launch them by name.
• `/edit-prompt` now opens an external editor from the full TUI, not only minimal mode.
• Up arrow on an empty prompt now selects queued follow-ups first instead of opening history.
• /plugin now works as an alias for /plugins in the TUI.
• Plugin-provided agents now appear in the /agents modal and can be toggled.
• /minimal and /fullscreen now switch instantly inside the running session without restarting or losing the current turn.
• The configurable status line row now appears at the bottom of minimal mode as well as fullscreen.
• grok clone now fetches only the selected branch tip by default, with --full-history for legacy full clones.
• grok clone can now reuse a matching local checkout as a linked worktree instead of always fetching from the network.

Bug Fixes:
• Subagent tasks are more resilient to temporary rate limits and will retry instead of failing immediately.
• Narrow allow rules for Bash commands now correctly permit file writes without extra prompts.
• Rules containing markdown headings now render correctly in the prompt.
• /new and /clear now preserve the last-chosen reasoning effort instead of resetting to the model default.
• Prompt dropdowns (slash, history, file search) now have consistent left alignment with the composer.
• History now shows every command, slash command, and memory note in the order you typed them.
• Collapsed tool-call rows no longer show a vertical accent line beside the status diamond.
• Hint text above the prompt now lines up with the text you type.
• Pressing Esc while peeking at a conversation from the dashboard now closes open modals instead of leaving the view.
• `/copy` now preserves markdown formatting such as headings and code fences.
• Sending a new message while a shell command is running now moves the command to the background instead of cancelling it.
• grok mcp add now correctly treats bare http(s):// URLs as HTTP servers instead of stdio commands.
• Plan mode no longer incorrectly blocks subagent spawns as file edits outside plan.md.
• MCP servers that share a URL but have different names are now kept as separate entries instead of being collapsed.
• Subagents and workflow-spawned agents no longer receive the workflow tool that only top-level sessions can use.
• Memory results are now presented as historical context that should be verified against live sources before use.
• Interactive grok sessions now start in ask mode by default again instead of auto.
• Minimal mode no longer truncates subagent wake-turn replies after the first token.

Performance:
• Concurrent subagents no longer trigger rate-limit errors during bursts.
• MCP server connections no longer delay session startup when many servers are configured.

content:
*We need all the scientific evidence on severe misalignment out in the open, urgently.*

TL;DR If severe misalignment is indeed emerging absent a high bar of alignment+control execution, the top priority actions for OpenAI and Anthropic in the next couple months should be to make public all necessary evidence for non-safety AI technical experts to become convinced of the science around loss-of-control themselves.

[the below is all my personal opinion and doesn't represent my employer]

Any meaningful solution to prevent loss-of-control-of-AI will require pan-US-AI-industry adherence to costly practices around AI control, alignment, and security. Crucially, this will include Meta, SpaceXAI, and even NVIDIA, and almost certainly require the blessing or coordination of the US government if it is to be internationalized. The current politics of AI make it unlikely that even OpenAI and Anthropic's joint technical consensus would be sufficient to motivate USG action so long as the lagging AI players are against it. Even if OpenAI and Anthropic were to go to the White House today with slam-dunk technical evidence of an imminent national security threat of AI loss-of-control absent intervention, the USG would probably not trust in their own in-house reasoning about that evidence, and would look to the views of the other admin-friendly AI players and advisors. These other actors appear largely skeptical.

The only solution is science.

title:
The UK Met Office has again been caught publishing temperatures from weather stations that don't exist. 

An FOI revealed Lowestoft closed in 2010, yet the Met Office kept issuing official temperature
content:
The UK Met Office has again been caught publishing temperatures from weather stations that don't exist. 

An FOI revealed Lowestoft closed in 2010, yet the Met Office kept issuing official temperatures for it. 

The office said they were using "well-correlated" neighboring stations, but the FOI revealed that this was a lie.

The numbers were actually coming from a model that was inventing data from 'phantom' neighboring stations. 

When exposed, they quietly deleted years of readings for Lowestoft, as well as a number of other stations, and added a disclaimer saying their data is "for general interest only."

FOIs also show over one third of Met Office stations never existed, and that real high-quality sites like Colwood are ignored. 

Also, more than 80% of the network is low-grade class 4 or 5, by WMO standards giving 2-5C uncertainty. 

This is the foundation of the UK's climate record – closed stations, imaginary stations and synthetic temperatures. The Met Office isn't credible.

content:
🚨 I think this news around Ox Alpha is much more important than it looks because its emergence says something much deeper about the actual state of the AI industry.

📈 Ox Alpha appeared anonymously on OpenRouter with around 1 million tokens of context, multimodal capabilities and extremely generous free access. It quickly attracted developers to the point where Stripe CEO Patrick Collison described it as “very impressive.” Some of the spectacular figures initially circulating were based on tiny samples, while broader evaluations are much more nuanced. However, an unknown player can now release a model for free that is good enough for the community to seriously wonder whether it comes from Google, Microsoft or one of several Chinese labs. Two years ago, that would have been hard to imagine.

🇨🇳 If Ox Alpha does turn out to be Chinese, market will wonder how many Chinese companies are now capable of operating close to the technological frontier. This clearly suggests that US semiconductor restrictions, while still highly constraining, are not preventing China from partly compensating through algorithmic efficiency, inference optimization and better use of available compute.

⚠️ For investors, the story becomes huge. If, in a few years, ten models can deliver sufficiently similar performance for 90% or 95% of use cases, the foundation model itself gradually becomes a commodity. A company will not pay ten times more for a few extra points on a benchmark as it will route requests toward the cheapest or most suitable model. The moat then shifts away from the LLM itself toward distribution, agents, proprietary data, software, cloud infrastructure and enterprise integration. This inevitably raises questions around the massive valuations of some pure-play AI companies, whose value still partly rests on the assumption that they will maintain a significant technological lead for a long time.

🤔 I think Ox Alpha is probably being underestimated because it may be another sign that the technological frontier is becoming increasingly crowded and that the cost of producing highly capable intelligence is falling much faster than expected. If we eventually find out that Ox Alpha is Chinese, uses materially less compute than comparable Western models and operates at extremely low inference costs, then it would be fair to ask whether the US AI industry is spending hundreds of billions of dollars building something whose economic rents are being commoditized far faster than anticipated.

At that point, it would no longer be just a technology story as we would need to start reconsidering how value is distributed across the entire AI value chain.

content:
Sam Altman:  "I think we should be more of a platform company than a product company.”

“We just merged ChatGPT and Codex together. So we used to have ChatGPT, Codex, and the API. And Codex, sort of unfortunately named, but that was not just coding, it could do any kind of work, which confused people."

“What I think most people want is the single interface to their own personal or their company's AGI that can kind of help them with whatever they need. And then the ability with an API to build anything they want on top of it. And that is the platform that we should offer to the world."

“We're going to sell great AI at every point on the cost-performance curve. You want really high end AI to discover science, that's great. You want really inexpensive AI to do a massive amount of volume of work that maybe doesn't require genius level intelligence, we got you covered there too.”

“I don't think we should go build every product category. I don't think we should go try to compete with all of our customers. I don't think we should try to subsume the entire economy. I think we should offer this platform and try to have 100 million new businesses and 8 billion people use it in all kinds of new ways."

content:
We need to normalize measuring and judging models against a standardized test harness

"Oh but model X performs best in their own proprietary harness"

I could not care less. When I take exams, I go to the standardized classroom, get the standardized pencil and exam sheet, and have to solve it under 2 hours

This system arose because we have a LOT of people to test

Guess what? We now have a LOT of models, and they are multiplying by the day

"Oh but model X performs substantially better in ARC-AGI-3 with a custom harness"

I don't care... Then imbue model X with enough knowledge so that it can reconstruct that harness on the spot

The main harness could be mini-swe-agent, terminus 2, vanilla pi or something along those lines

It needs to be simple, and stay roughly the same over time

There is already too much complexity in the benchmarking space right now, and I feel like not enough people are putting their feet down to cut away some part of it

制作に必要な処理を形にする側。

全部を手作業で編集する

AIごとに役割を分けて

TikTokに投稿。

完全視聴
751,649。

CTR
3.94%。

購入
3,412件。

最終売上
2,380万円。
さらに資料には
ORGANIC ONLY / NO PAIDとある。

広告を出して
無理やり表示回数を増やした結果ではない。
動画そのものが広がり
視聴され

リンクが押され
購入まで動いている。
ここで初心者が
勘違いしなくていいのが

「自分も182万回を狙わないと意味がない」
ということ。

最初からバズを狙う必要はない。

Codexで制作工程を補助する

投稿する

1本目を完璧にすることじゃない。
投稿したあとに

どこまで見られたか
どれだけクリックされたか
どこで離脱したか
数字から改善すること。

AIによって変わったのは
「ヒット動画を必ず作れる」ことではない。
試作品を作って
市場に出して
改善するまでのハードル。

これまで動画制作を
難しそうで避けていた人ほど
CodexとElevenLabsを触る意味がある。

作る側に回るための入口が
かなり広くなっている。

Claude Codeでそんなにトークンをガンガン使って何を作ってるんですか？とよく聞かれます。職種や部門ごとに作るべきものは様々ですが、マネジメントも含めて全員にオススメなのは「パーソナルエージェント」と「パーソナルナレッジベース」です。

パーソナルエージェントは自分の秘書のような存在で、毎朝モーニングブリーフィングとしてカレンダーの予定や未完了タスクや未読メールなどをピックアップして通知させ
content:
Claude Codeでそんなにトークンをガンガン使って何を作ってるんですか？とよく聞かれます。職種や部門ごとに作るべきものは様々ですが、マネジメントも含めて全員にオススメなのは「パーソナルエージェント」と「パーソナルナレッジベース」です。

パーソナルエージェントは自分の秘書のような存在で、毎朝モーニングブリーフィングとしてカレンダーの予定や未完了タスクや未読メールなどをピックアップして通知させたり、面接や会議、会食などの事前ブリーフィング資料をつくらせたり、日程調整をサポートさせたりします。

例えば会食だと、事前に同席する人の会社概要や直近のトピックス、その方の経歴や最新の発信、関心領域をDeep Researchにかけて調べたりしますよね。それをパーソナルエージェントが自動で実行するようにして、まとめたレポートを自分のみに権限設定したGoogleドキュメントに出力させて、Googleカレンダーの予定に添付させます。これはとっても便利。※もちろん、社内データを扱う場合はアクセス権限や保存先などのガバナンスをきちんと設計することが前提です

スケジュール調整なら、自分の好みを教えこんだ予定調整をしてもらえます。細かな移動時間を考慮させたり、金曜日は集中したいからなるべく入れないとか、面接や登壇はパワーを使うのでその後の予定はなるべくソフトにするとか、スコアリングロジックを自分好みに作り込むと提案の精度がとてもよくなってきます。

候補日を複数仮で入れて、決まったら確定させて仮の候補日を消すなどの日程調整系サービスがやるようなこともSkillを作れば自在にやってくれます。これを作り込んでからはあまりによすぎて調整系サービスを使わなくなりました。

パーソナルナレッジベースは、自分に関連するコンテキストやデータをためておき、RAG的に自由に質問したり、Deep Research的にレポートをつくったり、ダッシュボードアプリをつくったり自在にできるようにするものです。

Gemini Notebook(旧NotebookLM)でも同じようなことはできますが、ノートブックごとのソースファイル数に制限があったり、自分独自のデータ取得・加工フローをつくりこめない、出力の動作ロジックがブラックボックスでカスタマイズできないなどの不便さもあり、自作すると手放せなくなります。

関連するデータをわかりやすくフォルダに分けてダウンロードしておくだけでも、最近のモデルはいい感じに解析・動作をしてくれますが、データが増えてくるとカオスになりがち。

オススメは、「メダリオンアーキテクチャ」を採用することです。メダリオンとはオリンピックのような金・銀・銅メダルに由来する意味ですが、データをとにかく溜め込むBronze層、データを解析・構造化・正規化して扱いやすい形に整えるSilver層、KPI化や集計・分析などを行うGold層の三層に分け、欲しいアウトプットを生成させます。

例えばBronzeには取得したPDFやメール、議事録などの原本をそのまま保存し、Silverでは人物・企業・会議などの単位に構造化・正規化。Goldでは用途に応じてKPI化や集計・分析したデータを保存し、それをもとにレポートやダッシュボードなどを生成する、といったイメージです。

データ分析基盤のとてもベーシックなアーキテクチャですが、これを使うだけでデータ量がかなり増えても破綻しにくくなります。Bronze層は取得したPDFやPPTX、XLSXなどのデータそのものを触らず保存しておくことで、Silver層のロジックを変えてもいつでも再生成できることがポイントです。

この二つを作り込んでいくと、どんどんと大規模になっていきAIレベルがガンガン上がっていくはず。開発を効率化するためにloop engineeringやgraph engineeringに近いことをやりたくなってきて、関連ツールを自作したりと連鎖が止まらなくなって、つくりたいものだらけになります。

kubellの社内では「CEO’s AI Boot Camp」と題して私がコンテンツを作成したClaude Codeワークショップを定期開催しています。そのコンテンツのメインが、今回ご紹介したパーソナルエージェントとパーソナルナレッジベース。

小さくつくるのはそこまで難しくないので、毎日の業務の中から少しずつ育てていけるのがポイントです。ぜひ、チャレンジしてみてください！

content:
Robots are getting smarter. But there’s one thing they still desperately need: experience.
Think about how humans learn.
You don’t become good at driving by reading about cars.
You drive.

You make mistakes.
You correct yourself.
You repeat the process.
Robots need something similar, except at a much larger scale.

And this is where @axisrobotics becomes interesting.
Axis is building infrastructure focused on the training-data problem behind Physical AI.
Here’s the simple version:
• Simulation: People can interact with robotic environments directly through a browser.
• Data collection: Those interactions generate trajectories that can become training data.
• Validation: The submitted data is checked before it enters the training pipeline.
• Model training: The resulting data can be used to improve robotic policies.
• Real-world transfer: Axis has demonstrated community-generated simulation data being used to train a policy that was deployed on a physical robot. 

AXIS ROBOTICS
The bigger idea is fascinating.
Instead of having a small number of engineers manually teaching robots everything, Axis is creating a system where a distributed community can contribute to the learning process.

That changes the economics of collecting robotics data.
And with Axis V2, the idea goes even further: the robot attempts a task, humans intervene when necessary, and those corrections become additional training data. 
AXIS ROBOTICS
So maybe the real question isn’t:
“How smart can we make robots?”
Maybe it’s:
“How fast can we teach them?”
That’s the part of Physical AI I’m watching closely.
Graphic idea: Robot → Human → Data → Model → Better Robot.

title: This is a strong way to frame the real value of @axisrobotics because it shifts the conversation from data quantity to data quality. The biggest advantage is not simply having more contributors, but d
content:
This is a strong way to frame the real value of @axisrobotics because it shifts the conversation from data quantity to data quality. The biggest advantage is not simply having more contributors, but directing their effort toward the specific behaviors and failure cases that still challenge the model. That makes every successful correction more meaningful for improving the policy. 

Over time, this could make human feedback increasingly efficient as the system becomes better at identifying what it actually needs to learn. The contributor network essentially becomes an adaptive data engine rather than just a large source of demonstrations.

What I find especially interesting is the feedback loop created between the model and the contributors. As the policy improves, the easy tasks become less important because the system already knows how to handle them. Human attention can then move toward edge cases, difficult movements, and situations where the robot consistently fails. 

This creates a continuous process where contributors are not just producing data, but helping identify the next layer of problems that the model needs to solve. That could become increasingly valuable as robotic systems move toward more complex real world environments.

The verification component also matters because not every human intervention should automatically become training data. A correction becomes much more valuable when there is evidence that it actually improved the outcome of the task. 

This helps prevent the model from learning unnecessary movements or copying behaviors that do not contribute to success. The result is a cleaner connection between human effort and measurable improvement. That kind of filtering could be one of the key ingredients for making physical AI training more scalable.

The onchain trajectory requirement adds another interesting layer because it connects contribution with verifiable participation. Instead of simply completing a task and assuming it counts, contributors have a clear process for having their work recognized. 

This creates a stronger relationship between useful data generation, verification, and contributor incentives. If the system can consistently reward meaningful contributions, people have a reason to focus on quality rather than simply maximizing the number of submissions. That alignment could become important as decentralized robotics networks grow.

Overall, @axisrobotics is interesting because it treats human contribution as a resource that should become smarter over time. The goal is not to keep asking humans for more of everything, but to understand where their effort can create the greatest improvement for the model. 

If that feedback loop works at scale, the contributor network could continuously target weaknesses while the robot policies become stronger. That creates a compelling model where better AI leads to better data collection, which then leads to even better AI.

content:
Greetings gKaito family

But what if imperfect human data isn’t a weakness for robotics, but rather part of the scaling strategy ?

This might be my favorite finding yet from @axisrobotics .

Robot training often conjures up clean representations:

precise movements,
expert operators,
minimal error.

But crowdsourced data doesn’t seem to reflect this at all.

One person hesitates.

Another goes overboard.

One takes an inefficient path.

Another makes minor corrections.

At first glance, this seems like bad training data.

The Axis Sim Dataset V1 shows that something much more interesting is happening at scale.

If the dataset becomes large and diverse enough, these individual deviations aren’t necessarily aligned.

One operator shifts to the left.

Another shifts to the right.

While their noise might weaken across the distribution, the behavior they all share successfully completing the task is consistently reinforced.

AXIS tested this idea with community generated data.

Over 50,000 trajectories from Axis Hub were used for continuous pre training of π0.5.

Result reported in LIBERO Plus:

83.9% → 88.8%.

This result changed the question for me.

Instead of asking :

Is every trajectory perfect ?

perhaps Physical AI should increasingly ask :

Does the dataset have enough scale and diversity for useful behaviors to emerge from the distribution ?

And there's a crucial second part.

Scale can build a broad capability, but it can't solve every endpoint.

This is where Axis V2 gets interesting: let the policy expose its weaknesses, then use targeted human corrections via DAgger style feedback to address those failures.

So the cycle develops like this :

collect more data → train

to :

collect extensively → train → discover failures → finely correct → retrain.

This is a far more compelling Physical AI thesis than chasing the biggest dataset.

Perhaps the future isn't in perfect data.

Perhaps it's in extensive data + intelligent correction.

A robot failing once can be more useful than watching a human perform the task correctly another hundred times.

That distinction is becoming important in @axisrobotics V2.

Instead of treating data collection as a one-way pipeline, V2 uses human-gated DAgger: the policy attempts the task autonomously, while contributors intervene around failure points. Those corrections become targeted training data for the behavior the model actually struggles with.

This changes the data problem from “collect more demonstrations” to “collect the right corrections.”

For mature policies, that is a much more interesting optimization target. The dataset can increasingly be shaped by model weakness rather than by a static task list.

Data collection becomes part of the learning loop itself.

The more I explore @axisrobotics the more interesting their approach to Physical AI becomes.

Axis V2 introduced Human Gated DAgger, where robots handle what they can and humans step in when things go wrong. Those corrections then become valuable training data, creating a loop where every interaction can help improve future performance.

But the progress wasn't only on the product side.

Axis also announced a $12M Seed round, brought Professor Jiachen Li from Georgia Tech on board as Research Advisor, and introduced the Axis Point System to track and reward community contributions.

The product stack is also expanding with features like checkpoint save and rewind, articulated object interactions, TaskGen improvements, replay verification, OpenArm integration, and RoboCasa scenes.

What I find most interesting is how all of these pieces connect.

Task generation, simulation, human interaction, data processing, model training, deployment & failure feedback are being built into one compounding data engine.

And the scale is already showing.

Axis recently crossed 4M data trajectories on Base.

For Physical AI, high quality real world data could become one of the most important pieces of the puzzle.

Axis seems to be building around exactly that idea.

The next phase looks even more interesting.

title:
WikiHow Sues OpenAI Over Alleged Unauthorized Scraping of How-To Articles for ChatGPT Training

On August 21, 2026, wikiHow, Inc. filed a copyright infringement lawsuit against OpenAI and several rela
content:
WikiHow Sues OpenAI Over Alleged Unauthorized Scraping of How-To Articles for ChatGPT Training

On August 21, 2026, wikiHow, Inc. filed a copyright infringement lawsuit against OpenAI and several related entities in the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York (Case No. 1:26-cv-07171). 

The complaint alleges that OpenAI systematically scraped thousands of the site’s instructional articles without permission or payment to train its large language models, including those powering ChatGPT.

wikiHow describes itself as the internet’s largest library of human-authored, expert-verified how-to content, covering topics from everyday tasks to specialized skills. 

According to the filing, OpenAI copied more than 11,000 of these articles (with at least 1,211 registered copyrights at issue) either by directly crawling the website or incorporating them via third-party datasets such as Common Crawl. 

 I know it is in the Common Crawl as I am an expert on it and studied it in fine detail.

The company further claims that OpenAI’s crawlers continued accessing the site hundreds of thousands of times even after wikiHow implemented robots.txt directives blocking GPTBot, OAI-SearchBot, and ChatGPT-User starting in 2023 and expanded in 2025.

The lawsuit asserts that ChatGPT now generates competing how-to responses that closely reproduce the substance of wikiHow’s articles, often near-verbatim diverting pageviews, advertising revenue, and licensing income. wikiHow argues this substitution undermines the economic incentive to continue producing original content. 

Additional claims include intentional removal of copyright management information (CMI), such as titles, bylines, and copyright notices, in violation of the Digital Millennium Copyright Act.

OpenAI responded that its models are “trained on publicly available data and grounded in fair use.” The case seeks monetary damages (including actual damages, profits, or statutory damages), a permanent injunction against further infringement, and other relief.

This action forms part of a growing series of copyright suits by publishers, news organizations, and content creators against AI companies over training data practices. 

Similar cases have been filed by groups of newspaper publishers and others against OpenAI, Microsoft, and competing models. 

Court docket and complaint: https://t.co/dkzt4FMVea

title:
Handshake AI CSO @Sbhaiwala03 reveals how they build simulated white-collar work environments to train frontier AI agents:

"An environment consists of a few elements. The first is the software tools
content:
Handshake AI CSO @Sbhaiwala03 reveals how they build simulated white-collar work environments to train frontier AI agents:

"An environment consists of a few elements. The first is the software tools the agent needs access to. If I'm an investment banker, I have access to Excel, SEC EDGAR where all the financial reports are, and PowerPoint. Agents need the same access."

"We build simulated versions because of infrastructure and access constraints. Labs are querying that tool thousands of times in a given second."

"The second thing you need is data that populates the environment. If I'm building a financial model, I need the data room with the messy files from the company I'm evaluating."

"The final piece is tasks and verifiers. What are the requests of the agent that would reflect what a real investment banker might ask. We try to find tasks complex and realistic enough that the models fail. If the model can't perform, we know it needs more training data."

"What we send to labs is essentially a Docker file, a full containerized task. It has the tools the model has access to, the full data that populates the world, and the task and verifier. We'll send tens of thousands of these to a given lab for just one domain."

title:
Tackling a 60-year-old challenge in quantum chemistry: making density functional theory scale nearly linearly with system size.

This has huge implications for opening the door to realistic systems th
content:
Tackling a 60-year-old challenge in quantum chemistry: making density functional theory scale nearly linearly with system size.

This has huge implications for opening the door to realistic systems that have traditionally been too expensive to simulate.

AI has attempted to accelerate these calculations, but models generally struggle to extrapolate, particularly to systems larger than those seen during training. Unlike text or images, quantum-mechanical training data is extremely expensive to generate.

We present a single unified AI model that performs quantum-mechanical simulations of both molecules and materials in quasi-linear time.

Using a novel Fourier neural operator variant, we learn the underlying Kohn–Sham equation map to produce physics-informed, self-consistent answers.

Unlike prior AI approaches that directly predict chemical properties, our model works through intermediate steps to improve difficult predictions, resembling inference-time reasoning in large language models.

To demonstrate its scalability, we run a self-consistent calculation of a magnesium dislocation with about 80k electrons on a single GPU, which previously required about 7k GPUs.

content:
Most companies are stuck in what the industry is now calling "Death Valley" between POC and production.

99% of companies say they're deploying AI agents. 9% have. OpenAI's own enterprise data shows agentic products now account for 64% of corporate output tokens. The demand is massive, but the engineering to support it barely exists.

We've shipped 14 production agent systems in the last 12 months across healthcare and financial services. The same four engineering gaps kill the other 90%.

[1] Nobody builds a code graph, so the agent can't see how the codebase connects. It hallucinates function calls and invents APIs that don't exist.

[2] Nobody builds a knowledge base, so the agent has no access to internal docs or domain context. It answers from training data instead of yours.

[3] Nobody closes the feedback loop, so production errors go unlogged. The agent makes the same mistake on Tuesday that it made on Monday.

[4] Nobody builds approval gates, so the agent takes irreversible actions before anyone reviews them. One bad output goes to a customer before anyone catches it.

Every failed agent deployment I've seen died at the engineering layer.

We built what we call the Velocity Framework at @LimestoneHQ: code graph and knowledge base so the agent knows your system, feedback loops and approval gates so the agent learns and stays safe. 

A forward-deployed engineer builds it, trains the team to run it, and leaves.

From day 31, the agent compounds domain knowledge with each customer interaction.

The bridge across Death Valley is four pieces of engineering. 91% of companies haven't crossed it yet.

content:
Day 4 on @axisrobotics 

The more I look into Axis, the more I realize the importance of data quality over data quantity.

You can also see this in the results from the post-training data.

Out of 660 human corrections, only 161 which is 24.4% were useful to enter the training.

That’s not all.

Training on the full human trajectories dropped the robot success rate from 40.0% to 36.7%.

But when Axis trained only on the verified corrections, success increased to 48.3%.

And each useful training snippet was only around 0.8 seconds.

You can see that collecting more date doesn’t instantly make robots smarter.

I believe that a small piece of the right data can be more valuable than an entire trajectory.

title:
OpenAI proved that ChatGPT will always make things up.

It is mathematically inevitable.

They published a groundbreaking paper explaining why hallucinations are not a bug you can patch out. They are
content:
OpenAI proved that ChatGPT will always make things up.

It is mathematically inevitable.

They published a groundbreaking paper explaining why hallucinations are not a bug you can patch out. They are a permanent structural feature of how language models are built.

Think about how models are built and tested.

When an AI takes an exam or answers a prompt, how does the scoring system work?

If it gets the answer right, it gets a point. If it says "I don't know," it gets zero points.

Precisely the same score it gets for being completely, dangerously wrong.

Under that rule, the expected score for guessing is always higher than admitting uncertainty.

The industry evaluation methods do not reward accuracy. They reward confidence.

So the AI learns to gamble. When it doesn't know an answer, it doesn't hesitate or pause, it generates fluent, authoritative fiction because a confident guess has a chance of scoring points, while humility gets nothing.

Even if you feed an AI error-free training data, statistical pressures guarantee some error rate.

And because every benchmark on the market penalizes abstention, the models are literally optimized to lie to you with a straight face.

We are building high-stakes financial tools, medical systems, and corporate workflows on top of architectures that are mathematically incentivized to make things up when they are cornered.

The engineers can patch the symptoms. They can reduce the frequency.

But they can’t change the underlying law.

title:
the most important part of this week’s @axisrobotics update isn’t the 27 articulated object families or the 50×50 RoboCasa scene grid

it’s replay alignment

if a human trajectory works in the browser
content:
the most important part of this week’s @axisrobotics update isn’t the 27 articulated object families or the 50×50 RoboCasa scene grid

it’s replay alignment

if a human trajectory works in the browser but behaves differently when replayed by the policy server or physics engine, the training data becomes difficult to trust

the robot may appear to succeed during collection, then fail when the same action sequence is used for evaluation or training.

Axis says the browser, policy runtime and physics runtime are now aligned with full replay fidelity

that creates a much more reliable loop:

human collects a trajectory

→ system replays it consistently
→ data is evaluated and cleaned
→ policy performance is measured
→ useful corrections are filtered
→ improved behavior is distilled back into the model

this is what makes the next HG-DAgger training cycle more meaningful

the articulated assets and RoboCasa grid expand what TaskGen can generate

but replay alignment determines whether those generated tasks produce reusable data or just more simulation noise.

the real bottleneck in physical AI is not only collecting more robot demonstrations

it is making sure the same demonstration remains valid across collection, replay, training and evaluation.

that is the deeper signal from this week’s Axis update

That’s what I find most interesting about @axisrobotics latest post-training results

They collected 660 human corrections, but only
content:
More robot training data doesn’t automatically mean better robots.

That’s what I find most interesting about @axisrobotics latest post-training results

They collected 660 human corrections, but only 161 short snippets made it into training.

The surprising part is that the full human rescue trajectory wasn’t necessarily useful. It can contain pauses, unnecessary movements and actions the policy didn’t actually need.

The valuable signal was much smaller: the specific moment where the policy failed and the correction that helped it recover.

That’s a very different way of thinking about training data.

Instead of asking how much human data we can collect, the better question might be:

How much of that data actually teaches the model something it didn’t already know?

For Physical AI, filtering the signal may become just as important as scaling the dataset

title: As we build the next generation of biomolecular OpenFold models, we are looking to increase our staffing on both the scientific and engineering fronts. I thought it'd be worthwhile to write down our p
content:
As we build the next generation of biomolecular OpenFold models, we are looking to increase our staffing on both the scientific and engineering fronts. I thought it'd be worthwhile to write down our philosophy and what we're offering, as well as what we're looking for. If this resonates with you, please apply at the link below.

What we're offering:

True open source: we are contractually obligated by our funding streams to open source everything we do, including our training code infrastructure and training data, which no other group in the space has done. All the results we publish are fully reproducible with no missing "training enhancements" that keep the recipes hidden. We will not become a startup and we will not pivot to an API model. We are doing this exclusively as a public good for the public commons. Of course, commercial companies can and are encouraged to build on top of our models, but you will be contributing to an ecosystem guaranteed to remain open source.

Long horizon research: because we are not trying to turn a profit or satisfy investment trends, we can focus on hard problems that commercial labs are disincentivized to tackle. Our research vision spans years, not months, even while we release updates on a quarterly basis. This translates to problems spanning conformational ensembles, novel regions of chemical space, antibodies, nucleic acids, IDRs, macromolecular machines, and more.

Reach for the frontier: the open source ecosystem currently lags the industrial frontier by a few years. We aim to eliminate this gap. The two big deltas are engineering expertise and compute resources. We're doing alright on the latter, but it is the former where we need to grow. To make this possible we offer salaries and compute resources competitive with industry.

We are looking primarily for types of people, or the intersection of the two!

Machine learning scientists and engineers: people who have built and trained models at scale, whose command of the literature extends to the latent developments in efficient diffusion, optimization, recurrence, and reasoning.

Bioinformaticians and computational biologists: people who can assemble large and complex heterogeneous datasets, who write efficient data pipelines, and who deeply understand the structural biology domain.

If this is of interest to your network, please reshare. And if this interests you directly, please apply using the link below. This link is a catch-all site and so the job description and salary range are generic. It's there to help us streamline collection and review of resumes.

content:
AI企業が書籍を大量に購入し、スキャンした上で廃棄していることに批判的な言説の記事と投稿がまた流れてきたけども、文化的には違和感を感じるのはそれはそうだろうとして、米国著作権法と判例法から見ると、AI企業の経済的合理性追求とか野蛮さとかの問題ではなく、端的には訴訟リスクを下げようとした結果というのが大きいのだろう。

ここでのポイントは、書籍1冊 → 書籍1冊＋デジタル1コピー」ではなく、「書籍1冊 → デジタル1コピー」へ事実上の変換をすることになっていることであって、米国では適法に購入した紙の書籍の処分を購入者に認めるが、購入しただけで新たなデジタルコピー(複製)を作る権利まで得られるわけではない。その一方で、昨年のBartz v. Anthropicでは、Anthropicが適法に購入した紙の書籍をスキャンし、原本を廃棄して一対一でデジタル版に置換した行為について、コピー総数を増やさないフォーマット変換であること等を理由にフェアユースが認められた。

これとは逆に、LibGen等からの海賊版については同じ保護が認められず、巨大な訴訟リスクとなったわけであり、企業から見れば出所がよく分からないデジタルデータや契約の制約やDRM付きの電子書籍よりも、紙の書籍を適法に購入し、それを一対一でデジタル化して原本を廃棄する方が現在の判例に沿った法的に安全なデータ取得方法となっている。

まあ、その結果として紙の書籍を物理的に破壊する方向へ働いていることになるわけだが、これは現状ではそうなってしまうよなぁとしか。現状から変化する可能性もかなり薄いし。

content:
反AIの勝ち筋をAIにまとめてもらったよ。参考にしてねｗ
＝＝＝＝＝
反AIが本気で規制を実現したいなら、勝ち筋は「AIだから悪い」を捨てることだと思う。

AI生成物だから表示しろ、学習は全部許可制にしろ、では「Photoshopや検索・解析と何が違うの？」で詰まりやすい。

狙うべきは、AIによって新たに発生・増幅する具体的な被害。

・本人になりすますディープフェイク
・違法画像などを何度でも大量生成できる仕組み
・採用、融資、保険など重大判断のブラックボックス化
・AIを人間が過信する自動化バイアス
・被害が出ても開発者、提供者、利用者の責任が曖昧な問題
ここを「AI規制」ではなく、
ディープフェイク規制
高リスク自動意思決定の監査
被害者の削除・異議申立て・救済制度
必要時に検証できる記録保存
として要求する。
要するに、

「AIを禁止しろ」ではなく、「AIであろうとなかろうと、他人に重大な損害を与える仕組みには責任を負わせろ」

これならAI利用者とも共闘できるし、技術中立的で制度としても筋がいい。
反AIが一番勝ちにくいのは「AIだから嫌い」を法規制の根拠にすること。
一番勝ちやすいのは、具体的な被害を定義して、その部分だけを狙って規制することだと思う。

content:
コードレビューでトークンを燃やすのはもうやめよう、という記事
https://t.co/AqjswQeg4F

・人間とAIエージェントが安全かつ迅速にコードをリリースするための仕組みを模索した結果、結局カスタムリンターが最適だとわかった

・開発チームが生産するコード量はかつてないほど増えているが、検証プロセスがボトルネックになるため、コードを検証する速度を超えてリリースすることはできない
・粗悪なコードを大量に生み出すツールからシステムを守ることは、アーキテクトやプリンシパルエンジニアの最も重要な役割である

・人間とAIエージェントの双方に、高速で低コストなガードレールとフィードバックループを適用する必要がある
・チーム全体で週に数千件ものプルリクエストを作成するようになり、コードレビューの負担から開発者が疲弊するようになった
・CursorのBugBotというレビュー支援ツールを導入したが、重要ではないエッジケースを指摘したり、存在しないセキュリティの懸念に過剰反応したりすることが多かった
・BugBotの運用には週に約1000ドルの費用がかかる一方で、チームが大切にしているコード構造のガイドラインを全くチェックできず、かえって経験の浅いエンジニアが複雑なコードを書くようになってしまった

・そこでClaudeを使ってチーム専用のコードレビュー機能を構築し、個人のマシンで動かしたところ非常にうまく機能した
・しかし、その機能をGitHub Actions上で稼働させたところ、ノイズが多すぎてコードを読むよりもAIのコメントをレビューすることに時間を取られるようになり、1日で1000ドルのコストを突破したため即座に中止した

・AIが指摘したチーム独自のルール自体は有益だったため、高価なトークンを消費せずに同じようなチェックを高速かつ安価に実行する手段としてリンターに着目した
・リンターはコードの構文を数秒で解析してルールに沿った提案ができるため、LLMほどの高度な判断力はなくても費用対効果のバランスが最も優れている

・AIエージェントのFableに設計ガイドラインであるDESIGN.mdなどを読み込ませ、決定論的な部分を自動的にリンターのルールへと変換させた
・これにより、生のカラーコードの直接指定を禁止するno-raw-colorのルールや、ShadCNとBaseUIというデザインシステムの混在を防ぐチェックを容易に構築した
・さらに他のマークダウンファイルを読み込ませることで、不適切なログ記録を防ぐno-interpolated-consoleや、JSX関数のReactコンポーネント化を強制するno-render-helpersなどのカスタムルールを数多く作成した
・また、テストでの過剰なモック使用を避けるcheck_no_mockや、テスト名にアクター、アクション、エフェクトを明記させるcheck_test_namesなども構築した
・さらに、ドキュメント校正ツールのValeをベースにしたvale-de-blabというルールを作成し、コード内のコメントや仕様書から冗長な表現や受動態、AI特有の不自然な言い回しを検知して自動修正するようにした

・AIによるレビューはコメントが投稿されるまでに10分から30分かかるため、開発者がすでに別の作業へと移ってしまい、結果的にレビュー作業全体の負荷を増やしていた
・それに対して、リンターはもっとも遅いものでも27秒でチェックを終えてGitHubにコメントを投稿できるため、迅速に内容を確認して処理できる
・リンターは開発者のエディタ上でもリアルタイムにエラー箇所を波線で示せるため、コードを書いたその場で問題を修正してシフトレフト開発を実践できる
・さらに、コミット前のフックとして設定しておけば、開発を担当するAIエージェントがルール違反のあるコードを送信する前に、エラーを検知して自ら修正してコミットを再試行するようになる
・リンター自体は昔からある技術だが、AIを使うことで各チーム独自のカスタムルールを極めて簡単に作成できるようになった

title: The AI Patent Gold Rush: Volume, Value and Patent Strategy | IPWatchdog Unleashed
content: This week on IPWatchdog Unleashed, I spoke with Robert Plotkin, a patent attorney, computer scientist, and longtime software and AI practitioner. In what turned into a wide ranging conversation about artificial intelligence, Plotkin, who is the author of The Genie in the Machine and AI Armor: Securing the Future of Your AI Company with Strategic Intellectual Property, discusses the legal and strategic challenges confronting AI innovation. We discuss why companies should be cautious about treating AI patent counts as evidence of innovation leadership and why the most valuable AI patent portfolios are built around technology that matters to the business for a specific, articulable reason. title: Fifth Circuit Takes First Pass at Several Questions on Architectural Protections Under the AWCPA
content: On Friday, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit issued a ruling answering multiple questions of first impression regarding copyright claims involving building plans, including the scope of protection under the Architectural Works Copyright Protection Act (AWCPA) for constructed buildings and floorplan renderings. Vacating the Western District of Texas’ dismissal of Kipp Flores Architects’ (KFA) copyright infringement claims, the Fifth Circuit affirmed the lower court’s dismissal of KFA’s claims under the Digital Millennium Copyright Act (DMCA) over alleged failures to include copyright management information (CMI) on new floorplans developed from KFA’s technical drawings. title: Pay for What You Traverse: Ending After-Final Practice with Content-Based Fees
content: For many small businesses, uncertainty in patent prosecution can mean the difference between a strong issued patent and either abandonment or suboptimal coverage. One source of uncertainty in today’s system is final office action practice. Recent data suggests that roughly 42% of patent applications receive a final office action, meaning they are not allowed initially or after a response to a non-final office action. While receiving a final office action does not close the door on a patent application, it does give examiners greater discretion in directing its path. This discretion is unnecessary and can be eliminated by tying U.S. Patent and Trademark Office (USPTO) fees more closely to the actual content and complexity of each office action response. title: When the Quantum-AI Invention Stack Speeds Up Discovery, Patent Practice Has to Move Upstream
content: Artificial intelligence (AI) and quantum computing are compressing the invention cycle itself. That compression is no longer theoretical. Discovery Loop, a new public benefit corporation founded by leading former Google and Google DeepMind researchers, has announced a mission to automate experimental loops of the scientific method; the AItonomy Foundation similarly frames automated experimental loops as a path to accelerating science and engineering. The trend is also visible in Faraday, a recent AI model for automated scientific discovery that links model-driven hypothesis generation with iterative experimentation and R&D workflows, further illustrating how AI systems are moving from passive analysis toward active participation in the scientific method. title: Copying? Definitely. Infringement? Maybe.
content: A music photographer says artist Elizabeth Peyton turned his photo of Oasis brothers Liam and Noel Gallagher kissing into a painting, which sold at Sotheby’s for $1.92 million. Liam and Noel Gallagher of Oasis have spent three decades fighting with each other. Now a photograph of them kissing has started one too. Music photographer Justin Thomas took the photo at an Earls Court afterparty in 1995, at the height of Oasis’s Britpop reign and just after (What’s the Story) Morning Glory? turned the band into a global phenomenon. Earlier that year, Noel had reportedly hit Liam over the head with a cricket bat during the album’s recording sessions, so the kiss wasn’t exactly a representative sample of Gallagher family life. That contrast—two famously combative rock stars caught in a moment of seemingly genuine tenderness—is a big part of what makes the image so memorable. Thomas later ran a black-and-white version on the cover of his photo book, How Does It Feel? – Oasis 1995/2002 . What Thomas says he didn’t know was that, back in 1996, the American painter Elizabeth Peyton had made an oil painting of the very same kiss. The photograph on the cover of Justin Thomas’s book How Does It Feel? (L) and Elizabeth Peyton’s Earl’s Court (Liam + Noel) , 1996 (R) Peyton is a prominent contemporary artist who has long worked from photographs and other found images. Her Earl’s Court (Liam + Noel) depicts the brothers from the same angle and in the same pose as Thomas’s photo, right down to the ring on Liam’s hand near Noel’s collar. Her source has never exactly been a state secret. title: Child recruitment by armed groups surges in Colombia, rights group reports
content: Human Rights Watch (HRW) said Monday that armed groups in Colombia have increased their recruitment of children, citing what it described as an ineffective government response to the growing problem. In a report titled “ ‘I Thought I’d Never See My Mom Again’: Recruitment and Use of Children by Colombian Armed Groups , ” HRW examined the factors that place children at risk of recruitment and the methods armed groups use to recruit them. The report also examined the use of social media platforms , including Facebook and TikTok, to promote armed group membership and encourage children to join. HRW highlighted that 1,500 children have been recruited by armed groups in Colombia since 2021, with official figures indicating a sharp increase since 2023. The rights group noted that dissident armed groups are responsible for most of the reported cases, and that over half the cases have occurred in the state of Cauca. The report also found that indigenous communities have been disproportionately affected, accounting for nearly half of reported recruitment cases despite comprising approximately four percent of Colombia’s population. More than 30 percent of reported cases involved children between the ages of 10 and 14. Under international law , the recruitment of children under 15 by armed groups may constitute a war crime. Researchers have also reviewed more than 70 accounts and 40 social media posts that glorified armed group membership and encouraged users to join. Human rights organizations have called on the administration of President Abelardo de la Espriella to implement a comprehensive security and justice policy to address child recruitment. HRW also urged the government to provide sufficient resources and personnel to agencies responsible for combating recruitment, particularly at the municipal level. Tanya Chapuisat, the United Nations Children’s Fund (UNICEF) Colombia representative, has similarly called for increased protection for children

title: UN humanitarian chief warns increased drone use against civilians threatens Ukraine humanitarian response
content: UN humanitarian chief Tom Fletcher on Wednesday warned that the recent rise in the use of drones poses a risk for aid operations, emphasizing that international humanitarian law, which prohibits attacks on humanitarian workers and civilians, continues to apply to drone warfare regardless of how sophisticated or autonomous the weapons become. Fletcher, the UN Under-Secretary-General for Humanitarian Affairs and Emergency Relief Coordinator, spoke during a visit to Ukraine for World Humanitarian Day. After two days in Kherson, he described the city as “saturated by the use of drones against civilian areas.” He emphasized that humanitarian workers as well as civilian residents live under the constant peril of these weapons. Fletcher warned that as remote pilots move farther from their victims, so do accountability and justice. He also recounted a visit to a hospital where 70 percent of wounded patients were drone survivors, and witnessed the aftermath of a drone strike on Kherson Hospital. In a video posted to X , while driving the road from Mykolaiv to Kherson—known locally as the “Road of Death” because of the frequent Russian drone —the UN official remarked that “easily available means to kill are outstripping accountability.” Data from the UN Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine shows a sharp rise in civilian harm. In July 2026 , the estimated 437 civilians killed and 2,610 injured was the highest monthly toll since May 2022 . Missiles and drones accounted for 38 percent of casualties, with drones alone responsible for more than a fourth of deaths and causalities. While not the deadliest weapons in terms of overall toll, drones have contributed disproportionately to the recent surge in non-combatant casualties. Drones are cheap and flexible, allowing strikes both near and far from the front lines. Although drone technology is changing “every week” on both sides of the conflict, Fletcher stressed that “what doesn’t change or must not change each week is intern

title: Hong Kong court finds Tiananmen massacre commemorators guilty of subversion
content: The Hong Kong Court of First Instance on Friday found Chow Hang-tung, Lee Cheuk-yan, and the pair’s now-disbanded Hong Kong Alliance, guilty of a “subversion” offense under the Beijing-imposed National Security Law (NSL). They each face up to 10 years in prison. Three NSL-designated judges unanimously ruled that the defendants’ advocacy for “the end of one-party dictatorship” —primarily through annual June 4 vigils to commemorate the 1989 Tiananmen Square massacre— constituted “incitement to subversion.” They found that there could be no “natural end” to the leadership of the Chinese Communist Party (CCP); the advocacy must therefore constitute an incitement to overthrow or undermine China’s “basic system.” Chow and Lee argued at trial that all power belongs to the people under Article 2 of the Chinese Constitution . The court, however, pointed to the 2018 amendment to Article 1, which enshrines the CCP’s leadership as the defining feature of “socialism with Chinese characteristics,” China’s “basic system.” Thus, the organization’s advocacy was incompatible with the Chinese Constitution, amounting to unlawful “subversion.” As Article 18 of Hong Kong’s Basic Law provides that Chinese national laws do not automatically apply in the Special Autonomous Region, one issue the court faced was whether an act incompatible with the Chinese Constitution is unlawful within the territory. The judges wrote that the Chinese Constitution is the ultimate source of Hong Kong legal authority; national laws compatible with the “One Country, Two Systems” principle therefore apply in the city. The Hong Kong government welcomed the ruling, reiterating that the defendants were hostile towards the CCP and the Chinese government. Chief Executive John Lee vowed to safeguard national security and hold offenders accountable. Amnesty International

title: Amnesty International decries Argentina’s expanding AI surveillance as tool of social control
content: Amnesty International on Wednesday accused Argentina of building techno-authoritarian surveillance infrastructure without adequate legal safeguards, as the government’s newly created AI security unit expands state monitoring powers over citizens’ online communications and physical movements. In its latest report, the rights group stated that Argentina ‘s Ministry of Security spent at least USD $1.2 million on surveillance technology between 2024 and 2025, which included social media monitoring tools, facial recognition software, and thermal-camera drones with automatic tracking and ability to transmit images in real time. Amnesty expressed concern for the surveillance of protesters, journalists, activists, human rights defenders, migrants, young people, and marginalized groups. They warn that this can create a “ chilling effect ,” in which people who believe they are being monitored may avoid speaking, protesting or organizing, even without being directly arrested or punished. This raises concerns about the impact of surveillance on the right to freedom of expression, freedom of peaceful assembly, and freedom of association. In October 2025, Argentina bought a Clearview AI facial recognition license for USD $33,500. Clearview’s database contains more than 70 billion facial images scraped from the internet, and data protection authorities in France, Italy, Greece, and the Netherlands have already fined the company over its data practices. The Ministry, however, maintains that the Federal Police use facial recognition only in connection with active judicial investigations, and no evidence has surfaced that Clearview was used specifically to identify protesters. Argentina’s expansion of AI-driven surveillance has largely occurred through executive and ministerial measures. title: Minnesota Attorney General files suit against Texas governor over extradition of ICE agent
content: The State of Minnesota on Tuesday sued to compel Texas Governor Greg Abbott to extradite Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agent Christian Castro, who faces state charges stemming from an ICE shooting in Minneapolis last January. Minnesota Attorney General Keith Ellison and Governor Tim Walz sued in the US District Court for the Southern District of Texas, asking the court to bar Cameron County Sheriff Manuel Trevino from releasing Castro and order the governor to issue a rendition warrant. Texas law enforcement arrested Castro pursuant to a nationwide warrant on May 29. On June 2, Minnesota Governor Walz sent a request for extradition (also known as interstate rendition) to Texas Governor Abbott. The complaint alleges that Governor Abbott withheld the rendition warrant necessary to effectuate Castro’s extradition for nearly three months despite repeated requests, even as his office signed extradition warrants for Minnesota in other cases during the same period. Minnesota’s claims rest on the Extradition Clause of the US Constitution, the Federal Extradition Act, and Texas law. Article IV, Section 2, Clause 2, of the US Constitution requires that a person charged with a crime “who shall flee from Justice” to another state “shall, on Demand” of the governor of the state from which he fled, “be delivered up” to be sent back for prosecution. Minnesota argues that the Texas Governor’s withholding of the rendition warrant “lacks any lawful basis.” The Federal Extradition Act provides that upon presentation of a certified copy of an indictment or affidavit, the governor of the state where the fugitive fled “shall cause him to be arrested and secured” and delivered to the demanding state. title: The cat-and-mouse game over 3D-printed guns has begun
content: The creator of the world's first 3D-printed gun claims he's developed a way to thwart government-mandated software meant to block 3D printers from making firearms . It's an opening volley in what's shaping up to be an evolving battle between regulators trying to stem the tide of ghost guns and individuals trying to create workarounds. title: Zillow and Redfin settle FTC antitrust case over their rental listings partnership
content: The FTC and Zillow have announced a settlement that ends the case alleging that a 2025 "partnership" between Zillow and Redfin violated antitrust laws. The FTC had alleged Zillow agreed to pay Redfin to syndicate its listings, while Redfin would end its own advertising contracts and promise not to compete with Zillow for multifamily listings. The FTC's settlement proposal allows Redfin to continue syndicating rental listings from Zillow "unencumbered by the anticompetitive restraints" in the original deal, but also requires Redfin to restart its own rental listings advertising business, which it wound down as part of the partnership. title: EFF and Civil Society Groups Call on Nottinghamshire Police to Halt Live Face Recognition
content: This week, EFF, along with Big Brother Watch, Defend Digital Me, Liberty, Open Rights Group, Race Equality First, Statewatch, and Stopwatch, wrote to Nottinghamshire Police Force in the UK raising concern about the proposed roll-out of live facial recognition technology (LFR), and called for its immediate halt. In particular, the letter highlights six concerns: LFR Is Not "Just Another Tool" Nottinghamshire Police has stated that “facial recognition is just another tool to fight crime.” But LFR used in public spaces is an incredibly intrusive biometric mass surveillance technology that scans the faces of everyone who walks past the camera and takes biometric face prints. This is not just another tool, but a major escalation of surveillance that treats everyone as a suspect by default. People Having "Nothing to Worry About" Does Not Hold to Scrutiny According to Nottinghamshire Police, “if you aren’t entering the city or county to commit crime then you have nothing to worry about.” However, many people have legitimate concerns about the normalisation of invasive technologies. So a public that cannot move around their towns and cities without being subjected to a biometric identity check may be less willing to seek medical care or legal advice, speak with journalists, act in a union, vote, protest, or express their gender, sexual or religious identity. Disproportionate Targeting With LFR We are particularly concerned to learn that Nottinghamshire Police could deploy LFR to tackle low level crimes, such as youth behavior deemed anti-social, as part of Operation View. Reporting suggests that the force already possesses “a watchlist of young people believed to be causing the most problems,” including children as young as 11 years old. It would be highly disproportionate to deploy live facial recognition to tackle this behaviour. Many of these children are reportedly known to the police, and it is highly likely that there are more proportionate means for locating them. LF
author: Paige Collings

title: Intermediary Liability in Brazil: The Intricate Path Ahead
content: Brazil's new internet intermediary liability regime is underway. The implementation of changes established by the Supreme Court includes notice and takedown mechanisms and duty of care obligations. Caution is crucial as these measures can create problematic incentives for enforcement overreach and over censorship of protected speech. The court in June issued a new decision clarifying elements of its 2025 finding that the previous liability regime was partially unconstitutional. The government also published in late May two presidential decrees that detail how the new rules apply. Under the new regime, social media platforms and other internet applications that curate or interfere with posts can be held liable for third-party content if they don’t remove it after being notified by the user seeking take down unless there's a reasonable doubt that the content is unlawful. For certain specific cases, like crimes against honor (e.g. defamation), platform liability still depends on failing to comply with a judicial order. For some serious crimes, like human trafficking and crimes against women, applications have a duty of care to remove related content immediately and can be held liable when systemically failing to do so. The precise limits of what constitutes a systemic failure are still unclear. There are also stricter rules for paid ads, boosted content, and bots. The previous regime, set by Article 19 of the law known as the Brazilian Civil Rights Framework for the Internet (“Marco Civil da Internet” in Portuguese), sought to protect freedom of expression online by holding internet application providers liable for user content if they failed to comply with a judicial order to remove it. There were specific, limited exceptions to this rule, like the unauthorized disclosure of nude or private sexual images.
